newsitem.title: NIGERIA: FOCUS-Nigerians free 31 Shell staff, 96 still held.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nigerians free 31 Shell staff, 96 still held.

text.p: Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell said on Tuesday that 31 of its local staff and contractors, held by feuding communities in Nigeria, had been freed in a dispute that has also hit the U.S. oil company Chevron.

A company spokesman said in Lagos that 96 staff and contractors, all Nigerians, were still being held at Shell's six flow stations that have been occupied since last weekend by villagers protesting over the relocation of their local government headquarters.
"It is good news and we are getting somewhere but 96 others are still detained by villagers from the two communities," the spokesman said.

The dispute in which six workers have been injured also affected the operations of Chevron Nigeria. It said two of its installations in the oil-rich Niger Delta were picketed briefly on Saturday and Sunday by villagers, forcing a temporary reduction in production.
A Shell spokesman said the first 18 of its staff released included two who were among six injured on Saturday.
"Our supply boat left at midday today to pick (up) the injured based on an accord reached with the villagers," the Shell spokesman said before news that an additional 13 had been freed.
The company said three people had been injured on Monday night at one of the pumping stations in a fresh skirmish with the villagers.

The weekend attack made Shell shut down operations in the six stations and forced it to cut back production by 100,000 barrels per day of crude, about five percent of Nigeria's total output of almost two million bpd.
Nigeria is Africa's largest producer of crude oil, and with daily output of about 2.15 million barrels, ranks fifth in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
Shell, which pumps about half the country's total output, has often been the target of environmental protests and sabotage which forced its withdrawal from the Niger Delta's Ogoniland in 1993.

In 1994, Shell's Western Division headquarters in Warri was surrounded by protesters seeking a greater share of the region's oil wealth. A year later the spotlight again fell on Shell's Nigerian operations after the execution of Ogoni minority leader Ken Saro-Wiwa, who had led a campaign against the company's environmental record.
Shell said current protests were not directed against the company and that the villagers holding its employees and contractors had agreed to release all those injured in the disturbances.
"Our priorities are to evacuate the injured, release all the staff and then to reopen the stations," said a Shell official in London.
Shell said it had passed on a list of the villagers' demands to the local Delta State government in Nigeria and was calling for a calm and peaceful resolution to the dispute.
"Communications links have been re-established and we are continuing our dialogue with the community leaders," a spokesman said.
Despite the cutback in crude oil production, the company said export and other supply commitments were still being met.
World oil prices shrugged off the news of reduced Nigerian production and shares in Shell Transport and Trading also steadied, posting modest gains after shedding nearly two percent on Monday.
